Aram-Damascus.name: Aram-Damascus
Aram-Damascus.description: Aram-Damascus was the most powerful and best-documented Aramean kingdom, centered on the ancient city of Damascus in modern Syria. It rose to prominence in the 10th century BC and reached its peak under King Hazael in the second half of the 9th century BC, dominating much of the southern Levant before its conquest by the Neo-Assyrian Empire under Tiglath-Pileser III in 732 BC.

Zobah.name: Aram-Zobah
Zobah.fall: Defeated by David of Israel, later absorbed by Aram-Damascus
Zobah.description: Aram-Zobah was an important Aramean kingdom in the 10th century BC, located in the Beqaa Valley region between the Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon mountains. Under King Hadadezer, it was the dominant Aramean power before being defeated by King David of Israel and subsequently eclipsed by Aram-Damascus.

Beth-Rehob.name: Aram-Beth Rehob
Beth-Rehob.description: Aram-Beth Rehob was a small Aramean kingdom in the upper Jordan Valley or southern Beqaa region. It allied with the Ammonites against David of Israel and was later absorbed into the expanding kingdom of Aram-Damascus.

Maacah.name: Aram-Maacah
Maacah.description: Aram-Maacah was a small Aramean kingdom located in the area of the Golan Heights and Mount Hermon. It is mentioned in the Bible as an ally of the Ammonites against David. It was eventually absorbed by larger neighboring powers.

Geshur.name: Geshur
Geshur.description: Geshur was an Aramean kingdom in the Golan Heights region, east of the Sea of Galilee. It maintained diplomatic ties with Israel through marriage - King David married Maacah, daughter of Talmai king of Geshur. The kingdom was eventually absorbed by Aram-Damascus.

Tob.name: Tob
Tob.description: Tob was a small Aramean polity in Transjordan, mentioned in the Bible as the place where Jephthah fled and as an ally of the Ammonites against Israel. Its exact location and extent remain debated.

Hamath.name: Hamath
Hamath.fall: 720 BC (conquered by Sargon II of Assyria)
Hamath.description: Hamath was a major kingdom on the Orontes River in central Syria. Originally a Neo-Hittite/Luwian state, it became increasingly Aramaeanized from the 9th century BC. Under King Zakkur, it expanded to include Lu'ash. It participated in anti-Assyrian coalitions before its final conquest by Sargon II.

Luash.name: Lu'ash
Luash.fall: United with Hamath under Zakkur, then conquered by Assyria
Luash.description: Lu'ash was an Aramean kingdom in northern Syria, centered on the city of Hazrek (modern Tell Afis). It was eventually united with Hamath under King Zakkur in the early 8th century BC.

Bit-Agusi.name: Bit-Agusi
Bit-Agusi.description: Bit-Agusi was a major Aramean kingdom in northern Syria, founded by Gusi of Yakhan. Its capital was Arpad (modern Tell Rifaat). At its height it controlled territory from A'zaz to Aleppo. The Sefire treaty stelae document its diplomatic relations. It fell to Assyria after a three-year siege.

Bit-Adini.name: Bit-Adini
Bit-Adini.description: Bit-Adini was an Aramean kingdom straddling both banks of the Euphrates below Carchemish. Its capital was Til Barsip (modern Tell Ahmar). It was one of the first Aramean states conquered by the Neo-Assyrian Empire, falling to Shalmaneser III after its king Ahuni was defeated and deported.

Bit-Gabbar.name: Bit-Gabbar / Sam'al
Bit-Gabbar.fall: Became Assyrian vassal, then province (c. 713 BC)
Bit-Gabbar.description: Bit-Gabbar was the Aramean dynasty that ruled the city of Sam'al (modern Zincirli) in southeastern Anatolia. The site has yielded some of the richest Aramean archaeological finds, including the Kilamuwa Stele, Panamuwa inscriptions, Bar-Rakib inscriptions, and the Katumuwa Stele.

Pattin-Unqi.name: Pattin/Unqi
Pattin-Unqi.description: Pattin (also called Unqi) was a Neo-Hittite/Aramean kingdom in the Amuq Plain of southeastern Turkey. Its capital was Kunulua (Tell Tayinat). The kingdom shows a blend of Luwian and Aramean cultural elements.

Hatallu.name: Hatallu
Hatallu.description: Hatallu was a small Aramean polity in southeastern Anatolia. It is poorly attested and known primarily from Assyrian conquest records.

Bit-Bahiani.name: Bit-Bahiani
Bit-Bahiani.description: Bit-Bahiani was one of the earliest Aramean kingdoms in upper Mesopotamia, centered on Guzana (Tell Halaf) on the Khabur River. It produced some of the finest examples of Aramean monumental art, including the famous Tell Halaf sculptures and the bit-hilani palace of Kapara.

Bit-Zamani.name: Bit-Zamani
Bit-Zamani.description: Bit-Zamani was an Aramean kingdom in the upper Tigris region, near modern Diyarbakır in southeastern Turkey. It was one of the northernmost Aramean polities and frequently clashed with both Assyria and Urartu.

Bit-Halupe.name: Bit-Halupe
Bit-Halupe.description: Bit-Halupe was an Aramean tribal territory along the Khabur River in northeastern Syria. It was one of the Aramean groups that Assyrian kings repeatedly campaigned against during the early Neo-Assyrian period.

Bit-Hadipe.name: Bit-Hadipe
Bit-Hadipe.description: Bit-Hadipe was an Aramean tribal polity in upper Mesopotamia, known primarily from Assyrian royal inscriptions documenting campaigns against Aramean groups in the region.

Laqe.name: Laqe
Laqe.description: Laqe was an Aramean tribal region along the Middle Euphrates. It is described in Assyrian sources as both a tribe and a geographic area, frequently raided by Assyrian kings.

Suhu.name: Suhu
Suhu.description: Suhu was a region along the Middle Euphrates with a mixed population including Aramean tribal groups. Local rulers left inscriptions documenting conflicts with nomadic Aramean tribes passing through their territory.

Hindanu.name: Hindanu
Hindanu.description: Hindanu was a small polity on the Middle Euphrates with an Aramean population. It is attested in Assyrian sources as a waypoint on the route between Assyria and the Levant.

Bit-Yakini.name: Bit-Yakini
Bit-Yakini.description: Bit-Yakini was the most powerful of the Chaldean/Aramean tribal confederations in southern Babylonia. Under Merodach-Baladan II, it twice seized the throne of Babylon and challenged Assyrian hegemony over the region.

Bit-Dakkuri.name: Bit-Dakkuri
Bit-Dakkuri.description: Bit-Dakkuri was a major Chaldean/Aramean tribe in central Babylonia, located near the city of Borsippa. They frequently allied with or against Bit-Yakini in the power struggles over Babylon.

Bit-Amukani.name: Bit-Amukani
Bit-Amukani.description: Bit-Amukani was a major Chaldean/Aramean tribe in southern Babylonia, occupying territory between Nippur and Uruk. They were one of the three principal Chaldean tribal confederations alongside Bit-Yakini and Bit-Dakkuri.

Bit-Shilani.name: Bit-Shilani
Bit-Shilani.description: Bit-Shilani was a smaller Aramean/Chaldean tribe in Babylonia, attested in Neo-Assyrian sources alongside the major tribal confederations.

Bit-Saalli.name: Bit-Sa'alli
Bit-Saalli.description: Bit-Sa'alli was an Aramean tribe in Babylonia, mentioned in Neo-Assyrian inscriptions. Little is known about its internal structure or history beyond its attestation in conquest records.

Gambulu.name: Gambulu
Gambulu.description: Gambulu was an Aramean tribal confederation in eastern Babylonia, near the Elamite border. They frequently allied with Elam against Assyria and were involved in the major conflicts of the 7th century BC.

Litau.name: Litau
Litau.description: Litau was an Aramean tribal group in Babylonia, attested in Neo-Assyrian royal inscriptions as one of the Aramean confederations in the region.

Puqudu.name: Puqudu
Puqudu.description: Puqudu (biblical Pekod) was a prominent Aramean tribe in eastern Babylonia, living along the Tigris near Uruk and the Elamite border. They are mentioned in both Assyrian inscriptions and the Bible (Jeremiah 50:21, Ezekiel 23:23).

Itua.name: Itu'a
Itua.description: Itu'a was an Aramean tribal group in Babylonia, attested in Neo-Assyrian inscriptions. Their exact territory and political structure remain poorly understood.

Railu.name: Ra'ilu
Railu.description: Ra'ilu was an Aramean tribal group in Babylonia, mentioned in the inscriptions of Tiglath-Pileser III. Little is known beyond their attestation in Assyrian conquest records.
